messages.subject: Question categorical covariates
parts:
Hello,

I have a question on how to write categorical covariates in Stan. Indeed, in general (as in R for instance), if not specified as factor, the covariate is considered as continuous and the estimation is not the same if the covariate has more than 2 levels. I would like to know how to write this covariate in my model.

For example, let's imagine we have the following Stan code (that does not work for the moment), where "formule" and "formule2" are covariates with 3 levels, and we are in the context of a linear mixed effects model:

data {
  int N;
  int J;
  vector[N] y; 
  int num_indiv[N];
  int formule[N];
  int formule2[N];
}
parameters {
  vector[7] beta;
  vector[J] b;
  real<lower=0> sigma_b;
  real<lower=0> sigma_y;
}
model {
  real mu;
  b ~ normal(0, sigma_b);
  for(i in 1:N){
    mu = beta[1] + b[num_indiv[i]] + beta[2]*(formule[i]==1) + beta[3]*(formule[i]==2) + beta[4]*(formule[i]==3) + beta[5]*(formule2[i]==1) + beta[6]*(formule2[i]==2) + beta[7]*(formule2[i]==3);
    y[i] ~ lognormal(mu, sigma_y);
  }
}

Should I write the model like that? What about constraints on parameters beta?

Thanks in advance for your help !

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: Question categorical covariates
parts:
Hi Marie!

Usually you have one "reference level" which is made part of the intercept - I am not sure if you do that. This is the usual treatment contrast parametrization. I think your code should work - I would probably create a design matrix X for the fixed effect part. This can be don with model.matrix in R, for example. The biggest problem of your model is not using vectorization. So you better do

vector[N] mu;

for(i in 1:N) {
  mu[i] <- ... ;
}

y ~ lognormal(mu, sigma_y);

Or even better with everything put into matrices, etc. you should be able to write

y ~ lognormal(X * beta + Z *b, sigma_y)

.. of course, you need to setup X and Z in the transformed data or in R.

Also: either use standardized random effects b <- xi * sigma_b and xi ~ normal(0,1) OR use the centered version which would mean to include the mean into that normal(0, sigma_b) (replace it with normal(mu, sigma_b) ) - whatever is better depends on you data situation. If in doubt start with the standardized version I pointed out; known as the Matt trick or non-centered parametrization.

... or even easier: Just use rstanarm?

Best,
Sebastian

> model {

> mu = beta[1] + b[num_indiv[i]] + beta[2]*(formule[i]==1) + beta[3]*(formule[i]==2) + beta[4]*(formule[i]==3) + beta[5]*(formule2[i]==1) + beta[6]*(formule2[i]==2) + beta[7]*(formule2[i]==3);

That'll work. But it's not efficient. Much better to declare
the effects as a vector gamma and use:

beta[1 + formule[i]] + beta[4 + formule2[i]]

instead of

beta[2]*(formule[i]==1)
+ beta[3]*(formule[i]==2)
+ beta[4]*(formule[i]==3)
+ beta[5]*(formule2[i]==1)
+ beta[6]*(formule2[i]==2)
+ beta[7]*(formule2[i]==3)

And set the mu to be a vector mu[i] = ...

and then use

y ~ lognormal(mu, sigma_y);

without the index on y outside of the loop instead of
